extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers researching cultures/people unlike themselves (writers doing 'writing the other')
extracted.subtask_description: Practical research guidance for fiction writers who are creating characters or cultures unlike their own, focused on finding, evaluating, and triangulating sources to portray others respectfully and accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with your community library
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with your community library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Libraries are an underused resource; research librarians can help. Use the local library to locate accessible texts, request interlibrary loans, and get initial orientation to a topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulate between texts and sensory experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangulate between texts and sensory experiences like ethnic festivals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely solely on textual sources — back up reading with sensory, lived experience (attending ethnic festivals, events) to capture elements that texts may not convey. Prefer experiences where you are invited rather than intruding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for seminal textbooks and bibliographies
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for a good textbook — a seminal text students study — and then look at the bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use textbooks to get a 'lay of the land' and follow bibliographies to build a reading list. Repeatedly-cited works should be flagged for closer inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for biases — who and when wrote sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch for biases! Be aware of when and who wrote the books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider authors' backgrounds, era, and agendas (e.g., colonial/missionary perspectives, scholars who built careers on certain interpretations). Assess whether older seminal works reflect racial or cultural bias and account for that in how you use them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sit down and talk to people (community members)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sit down and talk to people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversations with people from the community you are portraying can provide lived experience and nuance. Use sensitivity readers for lived-experience checks. Approach respectfully and after doing foundational research so your questions are informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to scholars and specialists (after doing initial research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to scholars, too! First read the books, then talk to a specialist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend university lectures or events, then follow up with professors or curators who are often willing to talk. Do foundational reading first so you ask deeper, non-obvious questions and don't waste experts' time with basics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend public programming at universities and galleries
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities, art galleries, etc. have events. Go, listen, and talk to people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs, lectures, gallery talks and curator events are useful opportunities to learn and to meet specialists. Large cities especially provide more such opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare sources and go back to original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to find the source, the original source of something; go back to the first time that that was said in that book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary sources can misquote or paraphrase; tracing claims to originals can reveal differences in interpretation or context. If multiple works cite the same source, read that source for yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peruse quickly to filter and keep good track
rubrics_metrics.description: Open a book, take a quick look, look at a few pages, decide whether to keep it; cross out ones you don't need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an initial pile of potentially relevant works, then quickly scan to eliminate irrelevant items. Keep careful records of what you've checked to avoid duplication and wasted time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interlibrary loan and electronic databases to access rare/expensive works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use electronic databases and library loan for expensive or hard-to-buy books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many university-press books are expensive; you can often access them electronically or via interlibrary loan rather than purchasing. This expands access to otherwise unaffordable scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish primary and secondary sources; account for limited primary material
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your pile of primary and secondary sources, and be careful of when they were published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when primary materials are scarce (e.g., destroyed codices) and rely appropriately on post-conquest or archaeological records while noting their limits. Record publication dates and provenance to assess reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensitivity readers and community voices
rubrics_metrics.description: This is what sensitivity readers are for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After drafting or during research, use sensitivity readers from the relevant community to check for inaccuracies, stereotypes, and tone. Seek community scholars and practitioners for perspective, but still evaluate their views critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulate academic claims with contemporary practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare anthropological/academic accounts with contemporary practices to triangulate truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test historical or academic claims against present-day observed practices or interviews (e.g., comparing Witchcraft among the Azande with modern practitioners) to see what holds up and what is an outsider interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't automatically discount older sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't discount something just because it's old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While older works may reflect dated biases, they can still contain useful information (e.g., translations made with indigenous collaborators). Evaluate older sources on their merits and context rather than by age alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use references/bibliographies to judge an article's research depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing the references can tell you a little bit about how much research went into the writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long, substantive bibliography suggests deeper research; a lack of references may indicate a personal perspective or under-researched piece. Use bibliographies as a signal to follow up on sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer invited cultural experiences over intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: When researching sensory experiences, choose settings where you are invited to experience a cultural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnic festivals and community events where outsiders are welcome allow safer observation and learning. Avoid 'invading other people's spaces' without consent or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek 'own voices' scholarship and accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Own voices is important — people closer to the culture tend to bring deeper perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize voices and scholarship from community members or descendants for different insights, while recognizing that such sources can still have biases. Multiple perspectives are valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine multiple translations/editions for variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Read multiple translations (e.g., three versions of the Popol Vuh) and compare footnotes and translator approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different translations/editors can highlight different interpretations, especially when some translators collaborated with indigenous authors. Comparing translations can reveal nuances and missing context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to scholars' career-driven biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that scholars may have made reputations on certain biases; assess their work at arm's length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that an author's professional investment can color interpretations; evaluate claims critically and cross-check against other sources and community knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework: use historical press clippings as a research practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a news article or clipping from before 1980 as part of your research into something that interests you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using historical newspaper clippings helps you understand period perspectives and language. This exercise builds skill in locating primary-period sources and noticing historical framing.
